result: The authors developed 'thrifty' CNN models using 3-mer embeddings and convolutions that can achieve wider k-mer context (up to 13-mer) with fewer parameters than a 5-mer model, while providing modest performance improvements.
evaluation: Claims C5, C64, C115 demonstrate that a 13-mer model can have fewer parameters than a 5-mer model (supported by Table 1 data in C65). Claims C6, C77, C117 show modest performance improvements supported by Figure 2 data. The model architecture is clearly described in C56-C62 and illustrated in figures. The linear parameter scaling property (C63) is a mathematical consequence of the architecture.

result: Thrifty CNN models showed modest performance improvements over 5-mer and Spisak models on multiple metrics (AUROC, AUPRC, R-precision), with better performance on the tang dataset than briney dataset, attributed to differences in sequencing error between experiments.
evaluation: Claims C77, C95-C97 report performance comparisons supported by Figure 2 and Table 2 data. The surprising finding that tang data performed better than held-out briney data (C81) is explained by sequencing error differences (C82-C85), with the predicted underestimation pattern observed (C85). Claims C87-C88 note limited benefit from increasing model parameters, supported by the data.

result: Adding per-site rate parameters, positional encoding, or transformer components did not improve out-of-sample performance, contrasting with previous work by Spisak et al. 2020, which the authors attribute to differences in evaluation methodology and potential data leakage in the previous study.
evaluation: Claims C107-C108, C120, C127 report that various elaborations including per-site rates did not improve performance, supported by experimental results. Claims C121-C126 provide a critical analysis of why previous work found different results, identifying methodological issues (data splitting at parent-child pair level rather than sample level) and potential data leakage. Claim C129 provides a theoretical explanation for why per-site effects may be difficult to disentangle from motif effects.

result: Training on out-of-frame sequences versus synonymous mutations produces significantly different results, with models trained on one type performing poorly on the other, and augmenting out-of-frame data with synonymous mutations does not improve performance.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C111-C112 report the key finding that the two training approaches give different results, supported by Figure 4 data. Claim C113 concludes these capture different processes. Claims C134-C137 provide speculative explanations (codon usage bias, limited motif coverage, spatial correlation, selection on out-of-frame sequences), appropriately marked as speculation. The practical implication (C138) is noted.

result: Model fit assessment using overlap metrics and log likelihood showed all models performed similarly, with differences between models smaller than differences between datasets, though CNN models showed slightly better log likelihood on all held-out datasets.
evaluation: Claims C98-C103 describe the model fit evaluation methodology clearly. Claims C104-C106 report the results supported by Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The finding that model differences are smaller than dataset differences (C104) is an important observation about the limits of model improvement.

result: The study predicts SHM probabilities in parent-child sequence pairs derived from phylogenetic trees of out-of-frame BCR sequences, using a model that assumes site-independent mutations with per-site rates and conditional substitution probabilities.
evaluation: Claims C37-C43 clearly describe the research objective and data processing approach, with C41 illustrated in Figure 1a. Claims C44-C45, C48 describe the modeling assumptions, appropriately citing previous work. The rationale for using out-of-frame sequences (C40) is sound. This provides essential methodological context for the study.

result: The study used two main datasets (briney and tang) of out-of-frame IgH sequences, processed through phylogenetic inference with IQ-TREE using K80 substitution model and FreeRate heterogeneity model, with specific filtering criteria applied.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 introduce the datasets with appropriate citations. Claims C144-C162 provide detailed data processing methods including phylogenetic inference (C148-C150), filtering criteria (C146-C147, C161-C162), and sequence alignment procedures (C159-C160). The methods are clearly described and appropriately cite previous work and software tools.

result: Model complexity is limited by available data volume, and despite extensive efforts to find additional out-of-frame sequence data, no suitable large datasets were identified due to the rarity of out-of-frame sequences and limited full-length coverage in existing datasets.
evaluation: Claims C109-C110, C141-C142 state the data limitation and unsuccessful search for additional data. Claims C172-C175 provide detailed explanation of why additional data is scarce, with C173 citing database statistics showing >40% of sequences lack coverage at the V gene start. Claim C69 notes that hyperparameter optimization was not pursued further due to limited performance differences, consistent with data limitations.

result: The study evaluated models using AUROC, AUPRC, R-precision, and substitution accuracy metrics, with AUPRC chosen as less sensitive to class imbalance than AUROC given the rarity of mutations.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 correctly describe AUROC interpretation. Claims C72-C73 appropriately note AUROC's sensitivity to class imbalance and cite methodological papers supporting AUPRC as an alternative. Claims C74 and C76 define R-precision and substitution accuracy. These are standard metrics appropriately applied to the imbalanced classification problem.

result: Comparison with DeepSHM showed that the thrifty models achieved comparable performance with ~100 times fewer parameters and faster evaluation, with DeepSHM using 15-mers comparable to the thrifty models' 11-13-mers.
evaluation: Claims C89-C94 describe the DeepSHM comparison with appropriate citations. The parameter count comparison (C91) and computational efficiency observation (C92) are factual. The performance comparison (C95-C97) is supported by Table 2 data. This demonstrates the efficiency advantage of the thrifty approach.

result: The jaffe dataset of productive antibodies was processed to create a synonymous mutation dataset by masking non-fourfold degenerate sites in parent-child pairs.
evaluation: Claims C163-C167 clearly describe the jaffe dataset processing with appropriate citation (C163) and detailed methodology for identifying and masking fourfold degenerate sites (C165-C167). This provides a clear description of how synonymous mutation data was prepared for analysis.

result: Models were trained using a combined loss function of Poisson likelihood for mutation locations and categorical cross-entropy for base identity, with a 0.01 weight on the cross-entropy term, for 100 epochs using normalized mutation counts as offsets.
evaluation: Claims C168-C171 provide clear description of the training procedure including loss functions, weighting scheme, and training duration. The rationale for the 0.01 weight (C169) is to balance contributions from the two loss sources. Claim C171 notes an alternative joint optimization approach was also tried.

result: The authors released an open-source Python package with pretrained models and made the analysis reproducible via GitHub repositories.
evaluation: Claims C35-C36 state the software and code release with specific URLs. Claim C143 notes the reproducible analysis can be used for future data evaluation. This represents good scientific practice for reproducibility and community benefit.

result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about SHM, antibody biology, existing modeling approaches, and biological motivation for wider-context models.
evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C18 present established immunological knowledge about antibodies and SHM. Claims C19-C22 review existing SHM models with appropriate citations. Claims C23-C27 present biological motivation for wider context models, citing relevant mechanistic and recent work. Claims C28-C32 review existing wider-context approaches. This provides appropriate background and motivation for the study.

result: The modest performance improvement despite biological motivation for wider context is discussed, with the authors suggesting that while per-site and mesoscale effects may exist biologically, their impact is insufficient to significantly enhance statistical modeling performance, and more definitive conclusions require mechanistic models.
evaluation: Claims C117-C118 note the modest improvement is interesting given biological motivation, with appropriate citations. Claim C119 suggests the approach should capture features like nearby AID hotspots. Claims C130-C131 provide measured interpretation that biological effects may exist but don't substantially improve statistical models, appropriately citing mechanistic modeling work and acknowledging limitations of the statistical approach.
